Home prices are up[ 60
percent](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_The_State_of_the_Nations_Housing_2025.pdf)
since 2019, and purchasing the median-priced home would[ pose a significant
financial
strain](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_The_State_of_the_Nations_Housing_2025.pdf)
for most Americans.[ Half of all
renters](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_The_State_of_the_Nations_Housing_2025.pdf)
are cost-burdened, paying more than the recommended maximum of 30 percent of
their income on housing. Rising housing costs and a lack of affordable housing
has led to a[ record high level of chronic
homelessness](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_The_State_of_the_Nations_Housing_2025.pdf).

**There is not enough affordable housing:**

> \+ The nation faces a deficit of[ about 2 million
> homes](https://www.americanprogress.org/article/build-baby-build-a-plan-to-
> lower-housing-costs-for-all/) for purchase.
>
> \+ The median single-family home[ costs five times the median household
> income](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_The_State_of_the_Nations_Housing_2025.pdf).
> A cost of three times the median household income is what is considered to
> be affordable.
>
> \+ The nation faces a deficit of [over 7 million rental
> homes](https://nlihc.org/gap) affordable to low-income renters.
>
> \+ The number of[ lower-cost rental units is
> declining](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_The_State_of_the_Nations_Housing_2025.pdf),
> and new construction is[focused primarily on increasing the supply of
> higher-cost
> units](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_The_State_of_the_Nations_Housing_2025.pdf).
>
> \+ [About 80 percent](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/americas-rental-
> housing-2024) of renters in the lowest income quintile are housing cost
> burdened.

**Solution: Invest in Affordable Housing; Disinvest in Subsidies for the
Wealthy**

Federal housing policy directs too much funding to the wealthy and too little
for everyone else. For example, most of the benefit of the mortgage interest
deduction goes to[ households with incomes over
$200,000](https://taxpolicycenter.org/fiscal-facts/who-benefits-mortgage-
interest-deduction-and-who-misses-out), which is an amount[ _above_ the 80th
percentile](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2025/demo/income-
poverty/p60-286.html) in household income. The mortgage interest deduction
costs the government[ more than twice as much as the Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit](https://taxpolicycenter.org/fiscal-facts/who-benefits-mortgage-
interest-deduction-and-who-misses-out)(LIHTC). LIHTC housing, in turn, is a
better benefit for wealthy investors than for low-income renters. LIHTC
housing is generally[ more expensive for low-income
renters](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/Harvard_JCHS_State_of_the_Nations_Housing_2018.pdf)
than public housing. The Joint Center for Housing Studies finds that “LIHTC
[does not necessarily protect a renter from cost
burdens](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_Americas_Rental_Housing_2024.pdf),”
and “LIHTC units [often require additional
subsidies](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_Americas_Rental_Housing_2022.pdf)
to make this housing affordable.” Federal policy, however, has[ restricted the
creation of new federal public housing](https://nationalhomeless.org/repeal-
faircloth-amendment/) — the more affordable option — even though[ many people
have to wait years](https://cepr.net/publications/the-faircloth-amendment-
blocks-the-construction-of-affordable-housing-it-should-be-repealed/) to
obtain public housing. Instead of improving and increasing the availability of
public housing, there has been a[ steady increase in funding for LIHTC
housing](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_Americas_Rental_Housing_2024.pdf),
the more expensive option for low-income renters that benefits wealthy
investors. At every turn, federal housing policies are skewed toward making
the rich richer which makes housing more expensive for everyone else.

**The Public Wants More Investment in Affordable Housing**

[Multiple](https://www.searchlightinstitute.org/research/what-americans-think-
about-housing/) [polls](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-
release/2025/11/13/3187500/0/en/Heartland-Rasmussen-Poll-52-of-Young-Voters-
Have-Favorable-Impression-of-Democratic-Socialist-Zohran-Mamdani.html) show
that the public recognizes that there is a housing crisis because of an
insufficient supply of affordable housing. [More than four-fifths of
Democratic
voters](https://www.globenewswire.com/Tracker?data=4A5MuATX8BprCKHqrdaaIMwSra-
nhz4vco5K6oUHNEksAeLcxb12dRGFwEVzbb5yskwncmwdwG0pPZiXRdibuidkZ__-3YCcloRRJcpeVNdawGMsui21gsceGppovvH5jDnE-
tLwvNDnKSS4Ktru-W7KIJwrIUkM-
oYQnyXD76yO31_ITmqJVY3qD_bpnd5CDbArKuptgVljW5pHOKFvdg==) under 40 years old
believe that “the cost of housing in America [has] reached a crisis level.”
[Two-thirds of young Republican
voters](https://www.globenewswire.com/Tracker?data=4A5MuATX8BprCKHqrdaaIMwSra-
nhz4vco5K6oUHNEksAeLcxb12dRGFwEVzbb5yskwncmwdwG0pPZiXRdibuidkZ__-3YCcloRRJcpeVNdawGMsui21gsceGppovvH5jDnE-
tLwvNDnKSS4Ktru-W7KIJwrIUkM-
oYQnyXD76yO31_ITmqJVY3qD_bpnd5CDbArKuptgVljW5pHOKFvdg==) and seven-tenths of
other young voters also agree. A majority of the public support an increase in
government spending on affordable housing (see figure).
